title: Old Phones, New Lessons: India's Schools Tackle E-Waste
title_zh: 旧手机，新课堂：印度学校动手处理电子垃圾
source_name: India Today — “Schools collect 4.27 lakh e-waste items under Ministry of Education campaign” (25 Oct 2026)
summary_zh: 据《今日印度》10 月 25 日报道，印度教育部“生态俱乐部·LiFE 使命”框架下的一场全国电子垃圾宣传活动，从学校里收集了约 42.7 万件废旧电子产品（印度计数中的 4.27 lakh）。活动由巴贾杰基金会（Bajaj Foundation）与教育部学校教育与扫盲司合作开展，联合国儿童基金会 YuWaah 提供支持。共有 57,271 所学校报名参加，约 330 万人参与，其中学生约 302 万、教师约 27.8 万；25,731 所学校上报了收集情况，各地学校还设立了 39,494 个电子垃圾收集角。活动举办了 36 场线上讲座，讲解如何识别、收集、存放和运输电子垃圾，并指导老师寻找正规回收商、保护旧设备里的数据，还用各地方言发布资料。主办方表示，规定只有被理解和落实才有效，今后会继续与正规回收商合作并做好记录。
paragraphs: Think about the electronic devices in your home: an old mobile phone, a broken charger, a pair of headphones that no longer work. Most of us keep them in a drawer or simply throw them away. These items are known as electronic waste, or e-waste, and they are one of the fastest-growing types of rubbish in the world. Some of them contain harmful materials, but they also contain valuable metals that can be recovered if they are recycled properly.

In India, schools have decided to turn this problem into a lesson. According to a report by India Today on 25 October, a nationwide school campaign collected about 427,000 discarded electronic items. The campaign was part of the Ministry of Education's Eco Clubs for Mission LiFE programme, which encourages young people to adopt more sustainable lifestyles. It was run by the Bajaj Foundation together with the ministry's Department of School Education and Literacy, with support from UNICEF's youth platform, YuWaah.

The scale of participation was impressive. More than 57,000 schools reported taking part, and around 3.3 million people were involved, including roughly three million students and about 278,000 teachers. Over 25,000 schools reported collecting e-waste, and nearly 39,500 special collection corners were set up so that students and teachers could separate and store old devices safely.

However, the organisers stressed that collecting old gadgets is only the first step. Through 36 online seminars, schools learned how to identify, store, handle and transport e-waste. Teachers were also shown how to find authorised recyclers, how to protect personal data on old devices, and how to keep accurate records. To make the guidance easier to follow, information was shared in regional languages.

This point matters because rules alone rarely change behaviour. As one organiser from the Bajaj Foundation explained, guidelines have little effect unless people understand and follow them in practice. By involving children, the campaign may also influence parents, since students often bring new habits home.

The organisers say the work will continue through school sustainability activities and closer cooperation with recyclers. Their long-term goal is ambitious: to make the responsible repair, reuse and recycling of electronic goods a normal part of everyday life.
